title: Why is Switzerland never at war?
subtitle: Armed neutrality
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Two world wars tore Europe apart all around it, and Switzerland stayed out of both. Yet its neutrality rests on an army of conscripts, bunkers dug into the Alps and banks with a murky reputation.
author: ivana-toskovic

hero.hook: Neutral since 1815 and armed to the teeth: Switzerland does not fight wars, but it prepares for one every day.

blocks.text: In the heart of Europe, one country came through both world wars without joining either, which seemed impossible. In Switzerland, [[neutrality]] is not a passing policy but an old doctrine: the Peace of Westphalia recognized the Confederation's independence in **1648**, the [[Congress of Vienna]] its perpetual neutrality in **1815**, and the Constitution of **1848** confirmed it.

Switzerland has never joined the European Union, and it only entered the Schengen Area, which eases border checks, in **2008**. Above all, this country that refuses war keeps an army of conscripts, bunkers in the Alps and banks whose money has sometimes served other people's wars. How does the paradox hold?

sections.title: Neutral, but not indifferent: Geneva and the Red Cross

blocks.text: Neutrality is first of all a rule of international law. A neutral state takes no part in conflicts between other states and enters into no military alliance. If attacked, it may defend itself, but it does not meddle in other people's wars. The [[Hague Conventions]] of **1907** codified this law of neutrality, on land and at sea, and they remain a major source of international law.

blocks.caption: The alley of flags in front of the Palais des Nations in Geneva, the UN's European headquarters.

blocks.text: For Switzerland, neutrality is also an inner glue. The country brings together cantons of different languages and religions: staying out of Europe's wars keeps each one from siding with a camp and the country from splitting apart. As a mediator and a provider of humanitarian aid, Switzerland wants to prove that neutrality does not mean indifference. Geneva, home to the **UN** and to the [[International Committee of the Red Cross]], has become a capital of world diplomacy.
Geneva hosts the UN's European headquarters, but Switzerland itself only became a member in 2002. For decades, the host country stayed outside the door.

Neutral does not mean unarmed. Switzerland practices [[conscription]]: every male citizen must complete, from the age of **18**, compulsory military service of at least **245 days**. Refusing is a criminal offense, punishable by up to **18 months** in prison. In some cases, civilian service replaces the uniform. Those who do not serve pay an exemption tax.

blocks.caption: The entrance to a Swiss military fort, dug into the mountain and camouflaged.

blocks.text: Armed neutrality can also be read in the landscape. Tunnels and **bunkers** dug deep into the mountains are meant to deter any aggressor: attacking Switzerland would cost too much. These fortresses hold shelters, food supplies and all the logistics needed to survive any kind of attack.
In 2025, the Swiss voted on abolishing compulsory military service. **84%** of voters said no: armed neutrality remains a popular choice.

sections.title: Bank money, the dark side of neutrality

blocks.text: Neutrality has also made the country rich. After World War I, the **Swiss franc** was one of the few currencies accepted everywhere: it became essential to revive trade between nations. Under [[banking secrecy]], clients stayed anonymous, and Swiss vaults filled up with German money and Jewish money alike.

blocks.caption: Paradeplatz in Zurich, the heart of the Swiss financial center.

blocks.text: This is where the morality wavers. Can a country want to calm conflicts and profit from the money of those who wage them? Yesterday the assets of **Nazi Germany**, today millions linked to Russia's war in **Ukraine**: the financial center stands accused of laundering and sheltering dubious funds, money that has served to buy weapons or to help criminals escape justice. Neutrality protects the country, but it does not make it innocent.

sections.title: Facing NATO and the EU: a doctrine to redefine

blocks.text: Switzerland has joined neither [[NATO]], the Western military alliance, nor the European Union. Around it, neutrals are becoming rare. Since **Finland** and **Sweden** joined NATO, only three EU member states still declare themselves neutral: Ireland, Malta and Austria.

The country itself is divided. For some Swiss, neutrality is the heart of the national identity. Others argue for a less rigid doctrine and closer cooperation with the EU and NATO, in the face of new threats: **cyberwarfare**, or a spread of the war in Ukraine to the rest of Europe. Two centuries after the Congress of Vienna, Swiss neutrality has to be redefined.

events.title: Peace of Westphalia
events.detail: The independence of the Swiss Confederation is recognized.

events.title: Congress of Vienna
events.detail: The great powers recognize Switzerland's perpetual neutrality.

events.title: Hague Conventions
events.detail: The law of neutrality is codified, on land and at sea.

events.title: Switzerland joins the UN
events.detail: The country finally joins the organization whose European headquarters Geneva hosts.

events.title: Vote on military service
events.detail: 84% of voters refuse to abolish conscription.

blocks.text: Neutral since 1815, Switzerland does not fight wars but prepares for them: conscription, bunkers and discreet banks carry a doctrine that NATO, the EU and the war in Ukraine now force the country to rethink.
